O Śrotriya, by means of his instructional mantra, human beings who desire liberation find release in Kāśī;
having uttered it, human beings [attain their goal].
O Amṛta, I shall relate an ancient history:
in the region of Avanti, there was a certain Brāhmaṇa who was well-versed in the Vedas.
One who is endowed with learning and Vedic study is known as a *vidyādhara*;
[he belongs to] those wealthy ones such as the *śrotriyas* who are devoted to their private recitation and vows.
In his family, he was especially devoted to the performance of ritual bathing;
and he himself, along with the hosts of twice-born, was intent upon the recitation of the Vedas for him.
Having married a virtuous maiden of radiant smile from a family of Vedic scholars—
a woman renowned as Mandasā, beautiful in every limb— he [lived].

Having been initiated, that best of the twice-born constantly offered oblations according to the prescribed rules; yet, despite being such a man, he was excluded by those who followed the doctrines of the Vedas.
At one time, having reached an agreement there, he took pleasure in that number [of disciples],
abandoning the Vedic duties established by the Śruti and Smṛti.
He maintained constant association with heretics, was devoted to the wives of others,
became the husband of a courtesan, and was always intent on the expenditure of wealth.
Thus, as the wealth was being distributed among the brothers,
they remained constantly indifferent toward that twice-born man who had defiled the Vedas.
When his various possessions were lost, he remained devoted to his own wife;
his sister-in-law, consumed by a tumor, was brought to her death.
"O Hāra! O Rāma! O Rāma!"—uttering "Hāra! O Manohara!
he wanders upon the earth, making these sounds in many ways.
Thus, after much time had passed, Gatakalmaṣapañjara moved about as one liberated while living, by virtue of the greatness of his remembrance of Rāma.
Thus, impelled by Time, what do the servants do to that best of the twice-born?
Having agitated all his vital breaths, they [seek] to drag him out...
As he was being dragged away by the one of great splendor, he went to his destruction.
"The Vidyādhara was not seen here; where has that lowest of Brahmins gone?
Thus, their minds fixed on Śakti, they did not go [anywhere] among one another.
Having searched for a long time, the messengers, their faces covered in sweat,
reported to the king that the Brahmins were unable to perform the funeral rites.
"O Lord of the Pretas, having heard from the mouth of your attendant this speech,
we have come with speed to the presence of the Brahmin."
Having exerted great effort in our search for the brahmin, we saw nothing there; we have lost all hope for life.
"O great king, O Indra, we are indeed your obedient servants.
Having been told this, he then summoned Citragupta.
Yama said: "O Citragupta, you know everything, O omniscient one!
Today, [I shall hear] the conduct of this Brahmin named Vidyādhara."
And having reflected, [one should act] free from partiality toward the *ṇaka* school.
Having closely examined the multitude of leaves, Citra spoke these words to Daṇḍadhara:
"O Lord, O son of the Sun, listen to my words exactly as they are."
From birth onwards, a Brahmin who commits an assault on another's wife,
has sexual intercourse with a *vṛṣalī*, or likewise has sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman [is guilty].
Likewise, approaching a washerwoman, as well as approaching a dancer,
and also the wife of a bamboo-worker and the wife of a plasterer.
Out of intense passion, he committed adultery with the beloved wife of a tailor and that of a sawyer,
and even had sexual intercourse with a low-caste woman.
The wives of carpenters and other such artisans are called *ārūḍhapatikā* from the time they are born;
before the appearance of their menses, they are considered unmarried *brāhmaṇa* women.
Women married by one of the same lineage are declared by the wise to be *vṛṣalīs*.
Whatever merit a twice-born man might gain [by other means], he loses in a single night by discharging semen upon a *vṛṣalī*.
By constantly subsisting on alms, he is purified in three years;
however, a Brahmin who has sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells.
Because he violated another's wife, he is being cooked in the Kālasūtra hells;
this one, known as Vidyādhara, is the foremost among sinners.
He consumed forbidden food, as well as various kinds of meat,
and likewise the khaṭvāṅga, the mushroom, the śugrūka, and garlic.
O tiger, one should also eat niṣpāva beans, eat vyāghraparṇa leaves,
eat upotakī, and eat maurva with devotion.
Having committed such evils along with his wife,
he performed the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the *navaśrāddha*, and the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for the deceased.
That sinner against the brahmins even performed the acceptance of the gift of a cow;
having recited the Veda with a mere pretense, he was intent on receiving that gift.
He is a reviler of ascetics and likewise a detractor of the great;
he constantly and pointlessly commits such sins as these.
"Therefore, O twice-born one, you do not deserve the state of nirvāṇa in Videha.
When Citra had spoken thus, Kāla, the wielder of the staff, became enraged.
Taking hold of the staff-mudrā,
the king, who accomplished the task for the pretas, went into the presence of the Creator and reached Satyaloka.
Having prostrated before the four-faced one residing in Satyaloka, they praised him:
"Victory to you, O Lord of Speech, expert in the work of creation for the worlds!"
O ocean of compassion with four faces, known through the Vedas, pervading the universe,
you who perform the creation, preservation, and dissolution, and who bear the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
"Listen today to the petition of your servant, O worthy one.
Thus praised by Daṇḍadhara,
the Lord, the Sovereign of Speech, the source of the collection of Vedas, [spoke].
Seated upon his supreme throne and being praised by throngs of apsarases, he spoke to Kāla.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Umā-Saṃhitā.
Now begins the third chapter.
O Maheśvara, having approached Umā’s husband, what did the son of the Sun do? Please tell me out of compassion whatever was kept secret.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall relate the great life-story of the Brahmin;
having heard which, one is liberated from all sins and even from hell.
The one known as Vidyādhara attained liberation through union with the Divine among the Brahmins.
O Dharmarāja, I shall now recount the great life-story of that Brahmin.
By the mere remembrance of whom one shall become liberated while living—
this Brāhmaṇadāyoda, always remembering the name of Rāma.
O fair-faced one, the name of Rāma is equal to the *Sahasranāma*;
O auspicious lady, "Rāmacandra Bhadra" is a mantra equal to ten million sacrifices.
One should recite the mantra for Rāma, Rāmacandra, or Rāmabhadra, as proclaimed by the sage Namanta in the Vedāntas in their proper sequence.
A mortal who recites [this] for as long as life lasts is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, he of the Kauśika lineage recited the supreme mantra.
Citragupta:
By him all sins have been committed, both intentionally and otherwise.
For a sin committed intentionally, there is no expiation.
Devoted to taking the wives of others, the wealth of others, and the food of others,
he accumulated a store of riches solely through the deceitful speech of Vedic scholars.
Having accepted cows as a gift, he has sold them;
he is addicted to the practice of eating forbidden food and delights in improper acceptance of gifts.
Constantly attached to sense objects and excluded from pure conduct,
when the utterance of the word "Brahman" occurs, sin exits from his mouth.
When the recollection of the syllable *makāra* arises, they return to the state of ashes.
Thousands of killings of Brahmins, hundreds of thefts of gold,
hundreds of violations of the preceptor’s bed, and likewise hundreds of drinks of liquor.
Even hundreds of those associated with such people are liberated by the sight of Rāma;
even those who lack the domestic sacred fire (aupāsana) and are averse to the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña).
Even those who have neglected the twilight prayers become pure through the chanting of Rāma's name;
likewise, those addicted to eating forbidden food and those intent on sexual union with low-caste women [attain purity].
Constantly uttering the word "Rāma," whether walking, standing, sleeping, dancing, or even eating, those who possess such a mind are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
The twice-born is liberated by the chanting of the names of Raghunātha;
remembering the mantra at the beginning of the meal and with each morsel according to his inclination, he is freed. (p. 8)
Having proclaimed the victory of Rāma, the Kṣatriya swan is liberated.
That man on earth who utters the names of Raghunātha is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
One who recites even a verse, a quarter-verse, or even a single word of the Rāmāyaṇa at the end of meals is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
Those best of men who listen to the story of the Rāmāyaṇa alone,
having shaken off their sins, go to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Those mortals who hear this narrative concerning the desire for victory by Raghavendra— whether they hear a single verse, a single canto, or even a single chapter;
Human beings obtain the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices;
the Rishi has spoken twenty-four thousand verses.
Likewise, whoever hears or causes others to hear the entire Rāmāyaṇa— consisting of five hundred cantos, six books, and the Uttara-kāṇḍa— [attains the highest merit].
Liberated from all bonds, one is fit for becoming Brahman;
the sonless obtains a son, and the maiden shall find a virtuous husband.
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking wealth shall become wealthy;
and women who hear this while in their menses shall give birth to unsurpassed sons.
By hearing this Rāmāyaṇa, a barren woman shall obtain a son;
there shall be prosperity for the family and an abundance of wealth and grain.
Through the mere hearing [of this], there shall be prosperity for friends, as well as for sons,
and harmony among wives.
The acceptance of a great gift shall become a remover of great sins,
provided it is performed with reverence and according to the rule twenty-four times.

Whatever merit is gained from a six-year *kṛcchra* penance, whatever merit is gained from visiting the Setu, and whatever merit is gained from beholding sacred fords and mountains— that merit shall arise from listening [to this].
In certain sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, there is eligibility for only some;
however, in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa poem, there is eligibility for all.
It is held that one who is distinguished by the desire for liberation and other such qualities is entitled to the ritual action,
so that the means of accomplishing the obligatory rites and so forth may likewise lead to the knowledge of Brahman.
Likewise, there is no requirement for other means of accomplishment in the hearing of the Rāmāyaṇa;
by hearing this poem, the Rāmāyaṇa, men become partakers of liberation.
Just as the Gāyatrī is considered the most excellent because she is the mother of the Vedas,
so too is the narrative known as the Rāmāyaṇa, which consists of twenty-four thousand verses.
One who chants the Gāyatrī obtains dharma, artha, and kāma;
moreover, men on earth attain liberation simply by hearing it.
For living beings afflicted by the torments of saṃsāra and whose minds are despondent,
the nectar-like narrative known as the glorious Rāmāyaṇa shall serve as a medicine.
[This is] far from those whose tongues have been scorched, whose minds are destroyed by greed,
whose hearts are ruined by evil associations, and who are ensnared by the noose of the Kali age.
For those who are devoid of worship of the gods, who have abandoned the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti,
who are devoid of worship of the ancestors, and who also neglect the maintenance and worship of the sacred fires;
The story of the glorious Rāmāyaṇa destroys all sins;
those mortals on the face of the earth who listen to the glorious Rāmāyaṇa [attain liberation].
"Completely liberated from all sins, they shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu"—
thus spoke the four-faced Brahmā, renowned as the wielder of the staff (Yama).
Having heard the words spoken by the Creator of the Universe, Dharma turned back from the world of the Four-faced One;
surrounded by his attendants, he [went to] the city named Saṃyaminī.
Having gone to the city, he bowed down to the Creator of the Universe.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Umā-Saṃhitā.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Umā said: "Once again, I wish to hear of the majesty of the Lord of the Raghus—
how, having slain Rāvaṇa in Laṅkā, he established Vibhīṣaṇa there."
"What did Raghunātha do? You should tell me all of that. Śiva said:
"Having slain the ten-necked one in the midst of the ocean..."
Having mounted the vehicle dispatched by his mind,
he went to the city of Laṅkā situated on Mount Trikūṭa, along with the brother of Rāvaṇa.
Having made the king free from anxiety and having beheld Maheśvara,
Rāma was surrounded by bears, gopucchas, monkeys, and rākṣasas.
Having installed there a linga made of jewels for the Great Lord,
for the sake of removing the sin of killing a Brahmin and out of a desire to bestow grace upon the world.
Having seen the linga made of jewels, renowned as Rāmanātha,
they are cleansed of all sins and are glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having installed the great Liṅga for the removal of the sin of killing a Brahmin,
[he established] the Liṅga situated in the middle of the Setu, fashioned from gold.
Having beheld the Liṅga of Maheśvara, fashioned from great silver, renowned as Rāmanātha and the remover of all sins; (p. 12)
Released from the noose of ignorance, they attain the state of union (sāyujya);
moreover, on the northern shore of the ocean, there is an excellent sand-liṅga.
For the protection of the world and for the pacification of great sins,
Rāma established this Liṅga upon the summit of Mount Gandhamādana.
Upon seeing [this], a person is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
or else, for the cessation of the sin of killing a Brahmin, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance or the twelve-year penance.
Either the horse-sacrifice or the pilgrimage to Rāmasetu has been ordained by the sages,
who know the truth of the Vedas, for the protection of the world.
Sages declare that beholding Śrīśaila is equal to sixty kṛcchra penances;
likewise, they know it to be so from the sight of the one named Rāmeśvara.
Having broken through the triple-layered bridge with the tip of his quiver, Rāghava ascended the Puṣpaka chariot and departed toward the northern direction.
When the peak of Śrītīrtha, the lord of mountains,
had been reached at the hour of midday, Rāma descended from the Puṣpaka chariot.
Having invoked the celestial Gaṅgā and bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī at Tīrthagiri, that mortal performed a worship of Śambhu.
Having seen the linga of Tīrthagirīśa, he will be liberated;
ascending a celestial chariot adorned with jewels, he shall go through the sky to Mount Kiṣkindhā.
Having quickly descended from the Puṣpaka chariot and bathed in the river of auspicious waters,
he worshipped me, who am named Virūpākṣa, according to the scriptures.
The Kirāta worshipped me for a long time for the sake of my liberation;
having slain Vāli in battle, he became the lord of monkeys along with Vāli himself.
Having gone to the hermitage of Bharadvāja, Rāma, whose prowess is truth, bestowed liberation upon him by means of the fire of his arrows through me, who am named Rāma.
He dispatched Māruti to the presence of Bharata;
and having heard the words of Hanumān, Bharata, whose valor was true, [acted].
Followed by the citizens for a long distance, he went out from the city to meet Rāma;
Rāma, too, having been consecrated upon an excellent throne, went forth together with his brothers.
He carried out the protection of the kingdom according to justice;
he performed a hundred sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Having performed hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices as well as Bahusuvarṇaka rites,
he established the daily gift of ten thousand cows.
Every day, Rāma respectfully gave ten million gold pieces to distinguished Brāhmaṇas with the realization that it was an offering to Brahman.
The Brahmins were protectors of the Vedas who caused the countryside to flourish;
the kings were rich in great valor; and the Vaiśyas were lords of abundant wealth.
While Rāma was king upon the earth, even the Śūdras were devoted to giving;
such was the state of affairs under the most excellent of the Raghavas.
Day and night, he was overwhelmed by the thought of having killed a Brahmin; contemplating his own madness, he spoke these words to his father, Mitrāvaruṇa, who was born from his teeth.
Rāma:
O Preceptor, tell me the means for dispelling this heroic shame.
Vasiṣṭha:
Listen, O Raghava, O Indra among kings, to that which removes all sins.
Long ago, there was a low-born man named Kolahala who was impelled by Time.
Having slain his father with a sword and taken his mother, he departed;
reaching Vedāraṇya, he lamented, deluded by lust.
He too, through the power of Vedavaneshvara, by virtue of his devotion to Kshemarnava,
and due to the grace of Shiva, attained the knowledge of Vedanta.
"We have heard in the scriptures that [the sages] attained supreme liberation;
yet you, having gone to the forest of Vedavatī, have propitiated Vṛṣākapi."
"Having bowed to the Guru at the foot of the Śamī tree, you shall be released from the host of Gaṇas.
Thus addressed by her husband, Arundhatī [departed], and Rāma, together with his group of brothers, [proceeded].
Accompanied by his mothers and Sītā, and surrounded by a great army,
he departed from the Puṣpaka chariot toward Vedāraṇya.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli, and Kaśyapa;
Bharadvāja and Gautama—these were the sages who discoursed on Brahman.
Together with their disciples and grand-disciples, they were the followers of Rāma:
Dhṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, and Arthasādhaka.
Aśoka, Mantrapāda, and Sumantra went quickly;
the lord of monkeys departed accompanied by bears, monkeys, and gopucchas.
O beloved, having heard that Vibhīṣaṇa had gone to the Vedavana forest for the sake of beholding Rāma’s feet, he [Rāvaṇa] went there to increase the lineage of Khara.
Having descended from the Puṣpaka chariot, Rāma, dark as a blue lotus, quickly approached the bridge that had arrived near his head.
Having arrived according to the prescribed rule and bathed at Brahmatīrtha,
and then having bathed at Vedatīrtha, one should bathe at Maṇikarṇikā.
Having beheld the self-manifested Liṅga and bathed in that best of holy fords, he was liberated from the sin of killing a hero after having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Having given wealth to the Brahmins, he bestowed all manner of great gifts without exception:
jewels, gems, gold, and numerous elephant-gifts.
He established a city named Rāmacandrapura consisting of many villages,
and he installed a Liṅga under his own name that grants the accomplishment of all goals.
By the mere sight of that once, one is liberated from all sins—
whether joined with great transgressions (mahāpātaka) or joined with minor transgressions (kṣudrapātaka).
Having attained the Śrīrāmaliṅga, one shall become liberated while living;
Lakṣmaṇa installed this Liṅga for the removal of sins.
Hanumān also, having installed an excellent Śāmbhava Liṅga right there under his own name and having worshipped it, was liberated from the flood of his sins.
Having established a village endowed with many virtues on the beautiful bank of the Sahyajā,
the son of Vāyu was liberated from the sin arising from the slaughter of the Rākṣasas.
Having installed fifty great liṅgas here and there on the meritorious banks of the Kāverī, Rāghava worshipped them.
On the bank of the Paṃpā river, or on the bank of the Subrahmaṇyā river,
likewise on the bank of the Kṣura river, and similarly on the bank of the Peṇṇā.
Having established [the deity] here and there in meritorious regions— on the delightful banks of the Godāvarī and on the banks of the Revā river— the descendant of Raghu [proceeded].
Rāma carried out the protection of the kingdom in accordance with justice.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Umā-saṃhitā.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall tell you the fruit of the story of the Bālakāṇḍa—
the ascetic devoted to austerity and Vedic study, the best among those who know how to speak.
Vālmīki questioned Nārada, the bull among sages;
by hearing this with devotion, a person shall attain success through austerity.
A human being who is devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas attains its fruit;
liberated from the consumption of impure food, he becomes eternally purified.
Having heard this summary account, a mortal should cause it to be recited or read every day; thus, he becomes fit for union with Brahman.
O Goddess, for those who recite this at the conclusion of a meal, there is a great summary;
all their sins perish like the moon during the dark fortnight.
There will be an abundance of wealth and grain, as well as an increase in progeny;
there will also be an expansion of fields and gardens—of this there is no doubt.
One who is joined with self-restraint and endowed with the desire for the fruit,
reciting [the mantra] while remaining pure and eating sparingly, shall obtain the fruit of eighty *kṛcchra* penances.
From hearing [this teaching] a second time, one obtains the fruit described for reflection;
from hearing it even once, others obtain the fruit of meditative absorption (nididhyāsana).
"O Niṣāda, you have attained a lasting foundation for yourself for eternal years,
because you killed one of the pair of krauñca birds while it was deluded by passion."
Sent first by Brahmā, this verse issued forth from the mouth of the sage himself out of curiosity.
Therefore, this [work] should first be taught to children according to the syllables;
one who is proficient in all the sciences becomes beloved by all the gods.
Having become the foremost among eloquent speakers, he will wander through the worlds;
for formerly, this entire earth belonged to them all.
Beginning with Prajāpati, there have been victorious kings,
among whom was King Sagara, who was devoted to the dharma of his name.
In the great lineage of the Ikṣvākus, Rāma shall be king upon the earth;
from this has arisen the great narrative known as the Rāmāyaṇa.
I shall set forth this entire discourse in its full detail from the beginning;
it concerns dharma, artha, and kāma, and should be heard without malice.
By hearing this description of Ayodhyā, one is liberated from all sins;
all men shall become long-lived and partakers of the fruits of dharma and worldly prosperity.
By hearing the praise of a king's virtues, one is liberated from the faults of the king;
by speaking of the greatness of ministers, a minister is released from sin.
He found no one superior to himself, nor even an equal, let alone an enemy.
Those mortals who hear this [story] will indeed have no anger or other such passions.
Through extensive textual passages such as "But of that [Self] which possesses such power," and so forth,
there should be reflection on the well-spoken description of the Supreme Brahman.
Having stated "and north of the Sarayū," this is considered the *Vidisha* section;
it contains the narration of the virtues of Ṛśyaśṛṅga and the glorification of qualities such as peace (*śānti*).
For the purpose of bringing him here, Romapāda sent out well-adorned courtesans who were endowed with beauty and youth.
The sage fell under their control; what then can be said of an ordinary person?
Those who fear the terrors of saṃsāra must dwell in the presence of women.
Contact with them leads only to one's downfall;
it causes the decay of beauty, virtue, strength, and even wisdom.
It utterly destroys both the life and the reputation of women;
yet, from the arrival of the sage, a keen insight arises through his discourse.
One should properly honor Brahmins for the destruction of drought,
being peaceful, free from greed, devoted to dharma, and acting according to the rules with affection.
Of noble birth, endowed with beauty, possessed of virtues such as tranquility,
skilled in domestic duties, and devoted to the service of her husband.
O Goddess of Tripura, he who has such a wife as his householder shall indeed obtain all goals:
dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, the female class prospers therein;
such is the narrative of Sanatkumāra, as spoken by the most excellent of ministers.
Having heard this, a man desiring liberation shall attain the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya).
[This was said] by the king who, wishing to see a Brahmin in the city of Romapāda, [performed this rite].
By hearing of the attainment of his presence, one becomes heavy with [the weight of] a guru;
in every way, you shall obtain four sons by that number.
The meaning of the statement "He indeed goes to Yama" was previously explained by the poet;
the meaning of the Vedic passage beginning with "By sacrifice" arises from the commencement of the sacrifice.
In the meantime, the gods arrived at the shore of the Ocean of Milk, placing a brahmin at their head, for the sake of receiving their sacrificial portions.
Having gone there and heard that Hari, the wielder of the discus, according to the path prescribed in the Vedas,
O King, they— being severely oppressed by Rāvaṇa— offered their prayers to him.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you, the protector of the universe; salutations to the one who bears the conch and the discus.
You are praised by the seven Sāmans, O you whose eyes are like the seven horses of the sun."
O you who are worshipped by the seven [seers], O sole leader of the seven worlds,
salutations to you, the breaker of the seven *sāla* trees, to you who possess the seven garlands.
Thus praised by the host of gods, the illustrious Śārṅgadhanvā, blazing with an incomparable radiance,
beheld the multitude of the celestial hosts.
He spoke in a deeper voice.
Hari:
21) O bees, tell me, for what purpose are you here?
The gods, having reached the shore of the Ocean of Milk and being exceedingly exhausted,
approached Dhātṛ, Viṣṇu,
Varuṇa, and Yama.
Salutations to you, O God, Lord of gods, wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace!
O Lord, if you are to show favor to the inhabitants of heaven, please hear our petition.
Having heard this and taking it to heart, accomplish it, O treasury of compassion!
There is a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, born of the lineage of Pulastya.
In ancient times, at Gokarṇa, having propitiated this four-faced one,
the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, who was intent on afflicting the world, obtained boons.
Having conquered Indra, Time, Varuṇa, and the lords of the quarters,
and having seized their riches in manifold ways, he enjoys them in the city named Laṅkā.
Vahni was born as the liquor-seller Āndhasika; Śvasana became the house-sweeper Gṛhamārjuka; Varuṇa became the water-carrier Jalavāha; and Tumburu became the singer Gāyaka.
The Guru, having approached daily, declares the purity of the day;

those various [offerings] were made out of supreme reverence for the Creator of existence.
Out of respect for Mātali’s words, he discharged the Brahmāstra;
it pierced his heart, and he fell down and died.
The re-emergence of those who have been severed is due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā;
their death through the piercing of the heart was ordained by Brahmā.
Rāvaṇa wears an impenetrable armor upon his heart;
yet Rāma, having slain the grandson of Brahmā, acts for the protection of the world.

At Setu, he established the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha for the pacification of sins. Vibhīṣaṇa and the others duly honored the best of the Raghus, the slayer of enemies, with water for the feet, respectful offerings, seats, and salutations.
Having surrounded the destroyer of Rāvaṇa in battle, the hosts of gods in heaven placed that best of the Raghus, the enemy of the ten-headed one, upon their crowns.
They rained down showers of flowers born from the *sāntānika* trees;
having placed his arm upon the tip of the *triṇata* mountain,
his body was smeared with the dust raised from the field of battle.
Those who have accumulated a multitude of merits behold Rāma, his matted locks entwined and his lotus-face in full bloom.
With devotion, [worship] him who is accompanied by his friends, who has destroyed the ocean of enemies, who is a mine of compassion, whose bodily luster is dark,
and who is the preceptor in the initiation of the bow.
Those who worship them are the most fortunate on earth.
I bow today to the Primordial Guru, who bears matted locks and a blossoming, charming smile; whose left side is attended by the son of Sumitrā,
and who holds a bow and an excellent arrow in his hand.
The quarters became stainless, with their many afflictions stilled;
the Naga maidens returned to the world of the Nagas, and the Apsarases to the celestial abode.
Nārada, wandering about, approached Tumburu and Vṛṣaṇika;
meanwhile, Hāhā, Hūhū, and all the others had gone to the abode of Kubera.
The fire-god Agni went to the Gārhapatya hearth; Varuṇa went to Maṇīvata; Vāyu went to his own abode, and Soma returned to his own place.
The extent of the sun's own light, as well as the resting of the horses,
and the movement of the luminaries— these shall come to rest at midday.
Having heard of the honors bestowed upon the monkeys in the enemy’s city where Sītā dwells—
honors accompanied by uninterrupted joy— they rejoice like gods in heaven.
Having ascended the tip of the Puṣpaka chariot together with Sītā, Rāghava,
along with the monkeys and the Rākṣasas, beheld the Dūkkura mountains from there.
In a former kalpa, the all-pervading Mahādeva, the dancer at twilight, once showed his grace to Maya after he had praised him perfectly.
The wielder of the skull-bowl caused the end of the monkeys with his Pināka bow;
he brought about the destruction of the monkeys somewhere through the power of the Pināka.
When the fourteenth year was complete, on the fifth lunar day, having reached the hermitage of Bharadvāja, the disciplined Raghunandana paid homage to the sage.
By hearing these words, beginning with "p. 142)," all the undertakings of men shall be accomplished and the mass of their sins shall perish, until their formal coronation.
One who reaches the end of the Rāmāyaṇa undoubtedly attains an increase in sons, an increase in grain, and likewise an increase in wealth.
O Rāma, the noble one was seated upon the auspicious throne in the city of Sāketa,
together with sages who knew all truths, as well as his brothers and ministers.
Consecrated by the citizens, vassal kings, and royal princes, as well as by the Rākṣasas and monkeys,
he was graced with royal fortune and resplendent beneath a white parasol.
Adorned with priceless pearl ornaments and embellished with refined gold,
wearing yellow garments and garlands, he was anointed with divine fragrance.
Rāma, adorned with armlets and earrings, was always attended by Sītā;
the son of the Wind-god was the one who initiated his departure.
Having risen at dawn and performed his ablutions in the Sarasvatī river, he carried out the protection of the kingdom according to the principles of justice.
Rāma, smeared with ashes and adorned with a shimmering vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on his forehead,
looked into mirrors and other objects, and having completed his twilight rites (saṃdhyākarma), [proceeded].
Having duly worshipped the Lord reclining at Śrīraṅga with the resonant sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and the blaring of bherīs and paṭahas;
Placing Rāma at the forefront, they went toward the palace on the banks of the Sarayū; meanwhile, bards, genealogists, and panegyrists walked before the highly gratified descendant of Raghu.
Rāma, the lord of Ayodhyā, the destroyer of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa,
the establisher of all systems, and the promoter of all right conduct.
Thus, gladdening everyone with the sound of his horn,
the Lord Maheśvara, who is ever meditated upon by yogis, wandered about eternally.
Having offered oblations into the sacrificial fires, the constant giving of gold numbering ten million and a thousand fertile mares is proclaimed as a perpetual gift.
Having ruled the kingdom for ten thousand and one thousand years, Rāma will depart for the world of Brahmā.
For the sake of the continuity of the world, Rāma performed the consecration of many millions of Śiva-liṅgas according to the prescribed rites.
Permitted by Rāghava, the blameless assembly of kings,
as well as all the Rākṣasas and Vānaras, having stayed for a year and being granted leave by Rāghava, departed; Vibhīṣaṇa arrived [at Laṅkā].
At midday, for the sake of worshipping Viṣṇu, having placed Hari in the middle of the Kāverī according to the rules, he performed his daily bath and completed all his obligatory duties.
At that moment, the celestial chariot transformed into the form of the syllable Om.
The celestial chariot is shaped like the syllable Om (*praṇava*), with the Vedas as its peaks, and is most wonderful;
there lies the Blessed One, Śrīraṅgaśāyin, who reveals the welfare of those who bow before him.
If one should say "raṅga" when it is "raṅgam," or [say such] in cases of hunger, stumbling, and the like,
his faults will perish and there will be an increase in his lifespan.
Whether one has gone to another country or even to another island,
by turning toward Śrīraṅga and prostrating, one does not suffer.
And for the younger brother of Rāvaṇa,
who desired to uproot the stage and had entered as far as the netherworld (Pātāla), there was no strength remaining to support him.
O highly wise Vibhīṣaṇa, O Lord, do not despair;
this region of Sahya and Anūpa is dearer to me than Vaikuṇṭha itself.
O Vibhīṣaṇa, this incomparable place between the two rivers on the pure banks of the Kāverī is as delightful as the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
I desire to dwell right here, where happiness is granted through liberation to all;
for by the sight of Śrīraṅga, even all worms, insects, and moths [attain it].
O younger brother of Rāvaṇa, humans and even animals go to liberation;
I was formerly entreated by Ikṣvāku from my abode in Vaikuṇṭha.
Formerly, I dwelt in Ayodhyā, served by the descendants of Raghu;
now, served by you as well, I shall dwell here until the end of the kalpa.
O best of Rākṣasas, staying in Laṅkā during the month of Mādhava, when the moon is full,
he bathed in the waters of the Sahyā-born river and [meditated upon] Hari, whose abode is Śrīraṅga.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should offer a mango fruit accompanied by milk;
by that, O Rākṣasa, you shall obtain the fruit of a year’s worship.
O Goddess, Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, worships incessantly in the theater hall on the Vaiśākhī day for the sake of obtaining the fruits of the entire year.
For Raṅgadhāman, the lord of the Rākṣasas had a palace constructed by Viśvakarman according to the prescribed rites, adorned with seven enclosures.
Having worshipped the Goddess Śrī beneath the auspicious tree on the bank of the Candrapuṣkariṇī, Vibhīṣaṇa, instructed by Hari, reached Laṅkā.
Having bathed in the waters of the Kāverī and beheld the Lord reclining at Śrīraṅgam,
those who have attained the Fortune of Liberation shall become like the immortals.
He carried out the protection of the kingdom according to justice;
yet the Rākṣasas moved about in disguise, just like human beings.
The rain-cloud pours forth at the proper time, and the crops flourish in their season;
the kingdoms are well-nourished and indeed adorned with mines.
Freed from the grip of famine and devoid of the afflictions of bandits,
he who listens to the Rāmāyaṇa with devotion, even verse by verse or line by line, [attains liberation].
He who daily drinks [the nectar] with proper respect through the hollowed palms of his ears goes to the abode of Brahmā and is always honored by Brahmā.
The honey called the *Rāmāyaṇa*, flowing from the lotus-like mouth of Vālmīki,
[removes] birth, disease, old age, misfortune, and death, along with their extreme afflictions.
Having abandoned cyclic existence, that man goes to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu;
by hearing the Rāmāyaṇa even once, he shall never again be separated from his sons and kinsmen.
Upon hearing this, women who are menstruating shall give birth to unsurpassed sons;
and in the body of one who recites the Rāmāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu) resides.
Brahmā resides in my speech, Maheśa is in my heart, and I myself dwell within the heart; the sun and the moon are his eyes, and the deities reside in the pores of his skin.
The speaker should sit facing the east and the listeners facing the north;
having placed the son of the Wind (Hanumān) in front, the twice-born should worship him every day.
Having fed the twice-born according to one's ability with food accompanied by side dishes,
one should provide betel leaves to all the listeners.
Having bowed again and again to the twice-born, the king should listen to the words of the Brahmins.

Of this great mantra of the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*, Vālmīki is the seer (*ṛṣi*); the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chanda*); Śrī Rāma is the deity (*devatā*); *haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *saḥ* is the power (*śakti*). *Buddhi* is the seed-syllable; *jīva* is the power; *ilā* is the seed-syllable.

Piṅgalā is the Śakti. Sarasvatī, residing within the center of the Suṣumnā channel, is the Kīlaka. This is the application (viniyoga) for the purpose of attaining success through the grace of Śrī Rāmacandra during the recitation (japa). Oṃ Dharmātman, salutation to the two thumbs.
Satyasandha, salutation to the two index fingers. Rāma, salutation to the two middle fingers. Dāśarathi, [salutation to the two ring fingers].
Salutation to the two ring fingers: *anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ*. Salutation to the two little fingers: *pauruṣeṇāpratidvandvaḥ kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ*.
Salutation to the palms and backs of the hands: *śarair naṃ jahi rāvaṇiṃ karatalakarapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*. Thus is the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsaḥ*).
Meditation,
resembling a thousand [suns], is the destroyer of all enemies.
One should meditate on Rāma as consisting of power, and on Rāghava as the arrow of Rāma.
If Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is indeed righteous in soul, true to his promise,
and unrivaled in human prowess, then let him slay this Rāvaṇa with his arrows.
One should recite the mantra ten times and thereafter perform the Rāmāyaṇa; through the grace of Rāmacandra, [may there be success]. Śrī Rāma, Hari, is my refuge. Om.
